faqs.q: What should I do immediately after a car accident in {city}?
faqs.a: Call 911, document the scene with photos, exchange insurance information, and seek medical attention even if you feel fine. Do not admit fault. Then call FLM Law — we offer free consultations and can advise you before you speak to any insurance adjuster.

faqs.q: How long do I have to file a car accident claim in California?
faqs.a: California's statute of limitations for car accident injury claims is 2 years from the date of the accident (CCP § 335.1). Claims against government entities must be filed within 6 months. Do not wait — evidence disappears and witnesses forget.

faqs.q: What is my car accident case worth in {city}?
faqs.a: Every case is different. Compensation may include medical expenses (past and future), lost wages, loss of earning capacity, pain and suffering, and property damage. Cases in Los Angeles County frequently reach six or seven figures when injuries are serious.

faqs.q: Do I need a lawyer if the other driver was clearly at fault?
faqs.a: Yes. Insurance companies — even the at-fault driver's — are in the business of minimizing payouts. An experienced trial attorney ensures you don't accept a lowball settlement that fails to cover your future medical needs.

faqs.q: Who can be held liable in a truck accident in {city}?
faqs.a: In commercial truck accidents, liability can extend to the truck driver, the trucking company, the cargo loader, the truck manufacturer (if a defect contributed), and even the company that leased the vehicle. FLM Law's investigators identify every responsible party.

faqs.q: How is a truck accident case different from a car accident case?
faqs.a: Truck accident cases involve federal FMCSA regulations, complex insurance policies (often $1M+ in coverage), black box data that must be preserved immediately, and multiple defendants. Speed of action matters — trucking companies deploy investigators within hours of a serious crash.

faqs.q: What damages can I recover after a truck accident?
faqs.a: Medical expenses, future care costs, lost income, diminished earning capacity, pain and suffering, emotional distress, and in cases of gross negligence, punitive damages. Truck accident verdicts in California frequently exceed seven figures.

faqs.q: Can I recover damages even if I was lane splitting at the time of the accident?
faqs.a: Yes. California is the only state where lane splitting is legal (CVC § 21658.1). The fact that you were lane splitting does not automatically reduce or eliminate your claim. FLM Law has successfully recovered compensation for riders injured while lane splitting legally.

faqs.q: Do I need to wear a helmet to have a valid injury claim?
faqs.a: California law requires helmets (CVC § 27803). Riding without one may reduce your compensation under comparative fault rules, but does not bar your claim. An experienced attorney will minimize the impact of this factor on your recovery.

faqs.q: What do I need to prove in a slip and fall case in California?
faqs.a: You must show the property owner knew or should have known about the dangerous condition, failed to fix or warn about it, and that this failure caused your injuries. Documentation is critical — photographs of the hazard, incident reports, and witness statements all strengthen your case.

faqs.q: What if the property where I fell is owned by the government?
faqs.a: Claims against government entities in California require a Government Tort Claim filed within 6 months of the incident (Government Code § 911.2). Missing this deadline bars your claim entirely. Contact FLM Law immediately if you were injured on government property.

faqs.q: Is Uber or Lyft liable if their driver injured me?
faqs.a: It depends on the driver's app status at the time of the crash. If the driver was on an active trip, Uber/Lyft carries up to $1 million in liability coverage. If the app was on but no trip accepted, a contingent policy applies ($50K-$100K). FLM Law determines which policy covers your injuries.

faqs.q: What if I was a passenger in an Uber or Lyft that was in an accident?
faqs.a: Passengers are generally covered under Uber/Lyft's $1M liability policy regardless of fault. You may also have a claim against the other driver. FLM Law pursues all available coverage to maximize your compensation.

faqs.q: Who can file a wrongful death lawsuit in California?
faqs.a: Under California Code of Civil Procedure § 377.60, eligible claimants include the surviving spouse or domestic partner, children, and in some cases grandchildren and other dependents. The personal representative of the decedent's estate may also bring a survivor action.

faqs.q: What damages are available in a wrongful death case?
faqs.a: Surviving family members may recover loss of financial support, loss of gifts and benefits, funeral and burial expenses, and the reasonable value of household services. Separate survivor claims may recover lost earnings, medical expenses, and conscious pain and suffering before death.

statute_of_limitations: 2 years (CA CCP § 335.1); 6 months for government entities (Gov. Code § 911.2)

faqs.q: What qualifies as a catastrophic injury under California law in {city}?
faqs.a: California law does not define catastrophic injury in a single statute, but courts consistently treat spinal cord injuries, traumatic brain injuries, amputations, severe burns, vision or hearing loss, anoxic brain injuries, and polytrauma as catastrophic because of their permanent, life-altering nature. These cases require a dramatically different damages framework — lifetime cost projections, life care plans, and forensic economic analysis rather than simple past-expense tallying.

faqs.q: How long do I have to file a catastrophic injury lawsuit in California?
faqs.a: The general statute of limitations is two years from the date of injury under CCP § 335.1. If the defendant is a government entity, you have only six months to file a government tort claim under Government Code § 911.2. Evidence preservation is critical from day one — waiting even weeks can result in lost surveillance footage, destroyed black box data, and fading witness memory.

faqs.q: What is a life care plan and why do I need one?
faqs.a: A life care plan is a comprehensive, expert-authored document that projects every medical and support cost a catastrophically injured person will incur for the rest of their life — surgeries, medications, in-home care, adaptive equipment, home modifications, and vocational therapy. Without one, insurers make low offers based on past expenses only.

faqs.q: Can I recover damages for lifetime care needs if the insurance policy limit is too low?
faqs.a: Possibly. When the at-fault party's insurance is insufficient, we investigate every avenue of additional recovery: your own underinsured motorist coverage, umbrella policies, employer coverage, property owner coverage, and product liability claims if defective equipment contributed.

faqs.q: Who is at fault when a driver hits a pedestrian in a crosswalk in {city}?
faqs.a: California Vehicle Code § 21950 requires drivers to yield the right-of-way to pedestrians crossing in any marked or unmarked crosswalk at intersections. When a driver fails to yield and strikes a pedestrian in a crosswalk, they are presumptively negligent.

faqs.q: What if the driver who hit me fled the scene?
faqs.a: Hit-and-run claims can still be compensated even when the at-fault driver is never identified. California requires uninsured motorist (UM) coverage that applies to hit-and-run incidents, including for pedestrians and cyclists. We identify all available coverage and aggressively pursue the full recovery.

faqs.q: Does California require drivers to give cyclists three feet of space?
faqs.a: Yes. California Vehicle Code § 21760 requires drivers to maintain at least three feet of clearance when passing a cyclist. When a driver passes with less clearance and strikes or forces a cyclist off the road, the violation is evidence of negligence.

faqs.q: What is dooring and can I sue if a car door hit me while cycling?
faqs.a: Dooring occurs when a parked driver or passenger opens a car door into a cyclist's path without checking for oncoming traffic. California Vehicle Code § 22517 prohibits this. When a door strikes a cyclist or forces a swerve into traffic, the person who opened the door is liable for all resulting injuries.

faqs.q: What is premises liability in California?
faqs.a: Premises liability holds property owners and occupiers responsible for injuries caused by dangerous conditions they knew about, or should have known about, and failed to fix or warn visitors about. This covers negligent security, dangerous conditions, dog bites, and more.

faqs.q: Does California have strict liability for dog bites?
faqs.a: Yes. California Civil Code § 3342 imposes strict liability on dog owners for bites that occur in a public place or while the victim is lawfully on private property — regardless of whether the dog had ever bitten anyone before. There is no 'one bite' exception in California.

faqs.q: What if the property owner says I was trespassing?
faqs.a: Trespassing can reduce the duty of care owed, but property owners still cannot maintain conditions specifically designed to injure trespassers, and children are given special protection under the attractive nuisance doctrine. We evaluate the specific facts of your visit to determine your legal status and the owner's duty.

faqs.q: What is negligent security and how do I know if I have a claim?
faqs.a: Negligent security claims arise when a property owner fails to provide reasonable security measures — adequate lighting, functioning locks, security personnel — given a known history of criminal activity on or near the property, and that failure enables an assault or other crime against a visitor.
